newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Colombo port to earn $30 mln from P&O deal.
newsitem.headline: Colombo port to earn $30 mln from P&O deal.

text.p: The Colombo port will earn $30 million each year under a deal to lease a quay to a consortium led by units of Britain's Peninsular and Oriental Steam Navigation Co (P&O), the port chief said on Wednesday.

The port, South Asia's trans-shipment hub, needed to expand to meet rising demand that would outstrip current container handling capacity by 2000, Ranjith Wickramasinghe, chairman of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority (SLPA), said in an interview.
P&O had agreed to a 30-year lease of the Queen Elizabeth Quay (QEQ), said Wickramasinghe.
"The QEQ now makes a profit of $10 million a year," said Wickramasinghe. "Under the agreement being negotiated, the SLPA is estimated to earn $30 million a year from QEQ."

The project, on a build, operate and transfer basis, will be implemented by South Asia Gateway Terminals, a venture between P&O Navigation Australia, P&O Containers of Britain, Sri Lankan conglomerate John Keels Holdings and the SLPA.

SLPA's earnings would come from a $2.0 million annual ground rent linked to inflation, a $3 throughput rental per container and additional navigation charges of $8-9 per container, wharf handling charges of almost $13 per box and part of the storage rental on boxes, he said.
The SLPA would also earn dividends from its seven percent stake in the joint venture, he said.

South Asia Gateway Terminals would expand QEQ's container capacity to a million units a year from 250,000 currently, and simultaneously start building a new port adjacent to the existing one, Wickramasinghe said. Officials have said the new port will cost up to $1.0 billion.
"To remain in the hub port business we must have capacity to meet the demand. If not, we could lose the business we already have," he said.
The new port will have 11 berths capable of handling four million containers a year and a 15-16 metre draft to accommodate next-generation ships carrying 6,000 containers.
"Building a port takes time but we have immediate capacity constraints," said Wickramasinghe. "Also, ships being built now need deeper draft than the 13.5 metres of our present basin."
Colombo port last year handled nearly 1.4 million containers, up 29 percent from 1995, and is seen nearing its capacity of 1.6 million units this year.
"We anticipate a tremendous growth in cargo traffic with the liberalisation of India's economy and the containerisation of Indian cargo," Wickramasinghe said.
The port also hopes to attract traffic between India's eastern and western coasts and trans-shipment cargo from South Africa and even Western Australia, he said.

Trans-shipment traffic accounts for about 70 percent of the port's throughput. Trans-shipment occurs when a vessel discharges cargo at an intermediate port and the goods are unloaded to another ship bound for the final destination.
